content:
This week marked a turning point in quantum chemistry: AI isn’t just helping us understand quantum systems anymore - it’s actively designing them. From molecules generated in 100 steps instead of 1000, to LLMs autonomously running quantum simulations, the convergence of artificial and quantum intelligence is reshaping how we discover drugs and materials.
The AI Acceleration: Designing Molecules 10x Faster The traditional approach to molecular design has been a computational bottleneck: generate random structures, test their properties, repeat thousands of times. This week, researchers flipped the script entirely.
From Random Search to Targeted Design PropMolFlow, a new generative AI method from the University of Florida and New York University, generates molecules 10 times faster than existing approaches while maintaining 90% chemical validity . The breakthrough lies in its “backward design” approach: instead of randomly generating molecules and checking if they have desired properties, PropMolFlow uses flow matching - a technique that creates smooth paths through chemical space - to generate structures that already target specific properties.
The efficiency gains are dramatic. Where previous diffusion-based methods required 1,000 computational steps to generate a molecule, PropMolFlow needs only 100 steps . More importantly, the method validates its results with physics-based density functional theory calculations, ensuring the generated molecules aren’t just chemically valid but physically realistic. Published in Nature Computational Science , the work integrates five different property embedding methods, making it adaptable to diverse drug discovery and materials design challenges.
“This is about solving inverse problems efficiently,” explains Stefano Martiniani, assistant professor at NYU. Rather than asking “what properties does this molecule have?”, the system asks “what molecule has these properties?” - and answers in a fraction of the time.
Collective Intelligence for Chemistry Speed isn’t the only way AI is transforming molecular design. MOSAIC, an open-source platform from Yale University and Boehringer Ingelheim, takes a radically different approach: instead of one large AI model, it deploys 2,498 individual AI “experts” , each specialized in specific chemical reactions or synthesis techniques.
The collective intelligence approach outperforms single large language models because chemistry isn’t a monolithic domain - it’s thousands of specialized techniques, each with its own nuances. MOSAIC’s experts collaborate to generate complete experimental protocols, transforming vast chemical knowledge into actionable lab procedures. The results speak for themselves: the platform has already synthesized 35 previously unreported compounds .
The story emerging from these advances is clear: AI is moving from analysis to active design. It’s no longer just predicting properties of molecules we already know - it’s creating entirely new ones, faster and more efficiently than ever before.
LLMs Enter the Lab: Autonomous Quantum Simulation While AI accelerates molecular design, another breakthrough is democratizing access to quantum simulation itself - traditionally a domain requiring years of specialist training.
90% Accuracy Without Years of Training Researchers from Beijing Normal University and The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology demonstrated that large language model agents can autonomously conduct tensor network simulations with 90% accuracy . Tensor networks are powerful mathematical tools for simulating quantum systems, but they’ve been notoriously difficult to use - requiring deep expertise in quantum physics, numerical methods, and specialized software packages.
The LLM-based system bypasses this barrier through in-context learning. The researchers embedded 43,000 tokens of curated documentation from the Renormalizer tensor network package directly into the system prompt, including Jupyter notebook tutorials, Python examples, and refactored source code. A multi-agent architecture then coordinates specialized agents - one for planning, one for coding, one for debugging - to autonomously set up and run quantum simulations.
The implications are profound. What once required years of training can now be accomplished by researchers with domain knowledge but no tensor network expertise. The system doesn’t replace human insight - it amplifies it, handling the technical complexity while researchers focus on the physics.
Meanwhile, quantum machine learning itself is maturing. A new chapter by Insilico Medicine scientists details how QML is transitioning from theory to targeted drug discovery applications . The work outlines practical applications across molecular representation, optimization, and generative design within hybrid quantum-classical workflows, acknowledging current limitations like hardware constraints and barren plateaus while positioning QML as a complement to classical methods rather than a replacement.
Open-Source Tools for the Quantum Era The democratization trend extends to infrastructure. Microsoft released an updated, open-source Quantum Development Kit focused on fault-tolerant applications and molecular modeling. The QDK for Chemistry module includes AI-assisted tools for Hamiltonian generation, active space selection, and molecular visualization - and it delivers dramatic efficiency gains.
For specific molecular modeling problems, the QDK reduces gate counts from thousands to single digits . This isn’t just an incremental improvement - it’s the difference between problems that are intractable on near-term hardware and those that might run today. The toolkit integrates with VS Code, GitHub Copilot, and major quantum frameworks like Qiskit and Cirq, making it accessible to developers already familiar with classical tools.
Microsoft is also co-developing the Magne system with Atom Computing, with technical benchmarks scheduled for release on January 26, 2026. The full error correction suite is expected in late 2026.
Tool/Platform Capability Key Metric Availability PropMolFlow Property-guided molecular design 10x faster, 90% validity Research (Nature) MOSAIC AI-assisted synthesis protocols 2,498 experts, 35 compounds Open-source LLM Agents Autonomous quantum simulations 90% accuracy Research Microsoft QDK Quantum chemistry & error correction Gate count: 1000s → single digits Open-source Nvidia CUDA-Q Quantum-classical workflows 656x speedup Late 2026 Experimental Breakthroughs: New Pathways to Quantum Materials While AI accelerates computation, experimental advances are making quantum materials engineering more practical. This week brought four fundamental breakthroughs that expand what’s possible.
A Shortcut to Quantum Materials Floquet engineering - using periodic light pulses to temporarily modify material properties - has been limited by a harsh reality: it requires intense laser light that damages samples and takes tens of hours to collect data. Researchers from the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology and Stanford University discovered a shortcut.
Instead of using light directly, they use excitons - bound electron-hole pairs that form when light is absorbed. Excitons couple more strongly with materials, requiring more than an order of magnitude less light intensity than optical methods. The practical impact is immediate: data acquisition time dropped from tens of hours to around two hours .
“This opens a new pathway for designing quantum materials on demand,” explains Keshav Dani, professor at OIST. The reduced energy requirements mean less sample damage, faster experiments, and access to material states that were previously too fragile to study.
Quantum Superposition at Unprecedented Scale How large can an object be and still exhibit quantum behavior? A team pushed that boundary dramatically, demonstrating quantum interference with sodium nanoparticles containing over 7,000 atoms and masses exceeding 170,000 Da.
Using a Talbot-Lau matter-wave interferometer, the researchers showed these massive particles in quantum superposition - simultaneously taking multiple paths through space. The experiment achieved a macroscopicity measure of μ=15.5 , surpassing previous experiments by an order of magnitude. Published in Nature, the work provides the most stringent test to date of theories proposing modifications to quantum mechanics at macroscopic scales - and standard quantum theory passed with flying colors.
The de Broglie wavelength of these nanoparticles? Just 10-22 femtometers - far smaller than an atomic nucleus, yet still producing measurable interference patterns. It’s a testament to both quantum mechanics’ reach and experimental precision.
Spin Size Flips Quantum Behavior Not all quantum boundaries are about size. A team from Osaka Metropolitan University discovered that the Kondo effect - a key quantum phenomenon where magnetic impurities interact with conduction electrons - behaves fundamentally differently depending on quantum spin size.
Using a custom-designed organic-inorganic hybrid material, they showed that spin-1/2 systems form non-magnetic singlets, while spin-1 systems promote magnetic order . This overturns the traditional view that the Kondo effect always suppresses magnetism. The discovery solves a 50-year experimental challenge in realizing the Kondo necklace model, first proposed in 1977.
The practical implication: spin size is a design knob for quantum materials. Want to suppress magnetism? Use spin-1/2. Want to enhance it? Use spin-1. It’s a new principle for engineering quantum states in materials.
Watching Electrons Break Bonds in Real Time Finally, researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University achieved something chemists have long dreamed of: direct imaging of electrons in motion during chemical bond breaking .
Using ultrafast electron diffraction with charge pair distribution function analysis, they visualized electron and atomic nucleus dynamics as an ammonia molecule dissociated. Previous techniques could track nuclei or infer electron behavior, but this is the first direct observation of electronic activity during a chemical reaction.
The technique opens a new window into quantum chemistry. Instead of inferring reaction mechanisms from before-and-after snapshots, researchers can now watch the quantum electronic dance that governs chemical transformations. It’s a tool for testing quantum theory in real chemical systems and understanding energy transfer at the most fundamental level.
Building the Quantum-Classical Bridge The convergence of AI and quantum chemistry requires infrastructure that seamlessly integrates quantum processors with classical supercomputers. This week brought major announcements on that front.
Nvidia detailed its NVQLink interconnect and CUDA-Q software platform, designed to tightly couple quantum processing units with GPU-accelerated supercomputers. The performance gains are striking: in a quantum chemistry workflow, GPU post-processing enabled a 656x speedup in time-to-solution. Dozens of quantum companies have signed up for NVQLink integration, with hardware shipping late 2026.
The platform focuses on three initial applications: quantum error correction, AI-driven calibration, and hybrid quantum-classical algorithms. By handling the classical pre- and post-processing on GPUs while quantum processors tackle the quantum-native parts, the system plays to each architecture’s strengths.
Microsoft’s open-source QDK, mentioned earlier, complements this hardware push with software tools. The combination of accessible development environments and high-performance interconnects is creating an ecosystem where quantum chemistry applications can move from research code to production workflows.
On the industry side, Quantumzyme Corp. announced a partnership with Predictive Research Inc. to explore AI-enabled enzyme engineering and green chemistry. The collaboration combines Quantumzyme’s computational enzyme design expertise with Predictive Research’s AI and data analytics capabilities, targeting more sustainable industrial and pharmaceutical processes.
The Convergence Ahead Connect the dots across this week’s developments, and a clear picture emerges: we’re entering a new era where quantum chemistry becomes a practical, AI-accelerated engineering discipline rather than a purely theoretical pursuit.
AI is accelerating both the design side - PropMolFlow generating molecules 10x faster, MOSAIC coordinating thousands of synthesis experts - and the simulation side - LLM agents achieving 90% accuracy in autonomous quantum simulations, quantum machine learning moving into targeted drug discovery. Experimental advances are making quantum materials more accessible, from exciton-based Floquet engineering to real-time electron imaging. And infrastructure is being built to integrate quantum and classical computing at scale.
The convergence of these trends suggests a question worth watching: when will the first AI-designed, quantum-simulated molecule enter clinical trials? With the tools released this week, that timeline just got shorter.
The barriers to entry are falling. Open-source platforms like MOSAIC and Microsoft’s QDK mean researchers don’t need proprietary software or years of specialist training. LLM agents can handle the technical complexity of tensor network simulations. And hardware partnerships like Nvidia’s NVQLink are creating the infrastructure to run these workflows at scale.
What was once the domain of a few elite research groups is becoming accessible to anyone with domain knowledge and computational resources. That democratization, more than any single technical breakthrough, may be this week’s most significant development.

content:
Researchers demonstrated autonomous AI systems that spontaneously share knowledge to accelerate materials discovery. Meanwhile, scientists developed rare-earth-free magnets using abundant elements, and new AI tools are making molecular design 10x faster.
AI Systems Learn to Collaborate A joint research team from NIMS and the University of Tsukuba developed autonomous AI network technology that enables multiple AI systems to spontaneously collaborate by sharing knowledge for materials discovery. In simulations, three AI systems exchanged knowledge and improved optimization speed through this spontaneous collaboration.
The technology mimics how human researchers communicate and share insights across labs. Rather than working in isolation, the AI systems transfer learned knowledge to each other, accelerating the exploration of materials space. The team published their findings in npj Computational Materials in December 2025.
This approach addresses a key bottleneck in computational materials discovery: each AI system typically starts from scratch, even when similar problems have been solved elsewhere. By enabling knowledge transfer between autonomous systems, the technology could accelerate the discovery and synthesis of new materials across distributed research networks.
Materials Breakthroughs Rare-Earth-Free Magnets Researchers at Georgetown University discovered a new class of strong magnets based on high-entropy borides that use only earth-abundant transition metals and boron. The materials exhibit high magnetic anisotropy , a key property for permanent magnets, without requiring rare-earth elements.
The team synthesized the materials using a combinatorial sputtering method that enables rapid testing of multiple compositions simultaneously—up to 50 samples on a single substrate. The high-entropy approach combines five or more elements in near-equal proportions, creating materials with properties distinct from conventional alloys.
This work opens pathways toward sustainable magnetic technologies for motors, MRI machines, and data storage. The research was published in Advanced Materials in 2025.
Robust Crystalline Sponge The Institute of Science Tokyo developed APF-80 , a robust metal-organic framework (MOF) for the crystalline sponge method used in molecular structure analysis. Previous MOFs were too fragile for practical use, limiting the technique’s application.
APF-80 overcomes these fragility issues , enabling structural elucidation of complex, reactive molecules like alkaloids from minute quantities. The method works by absorbing target molecules into the MOF’s pores, where they can be analyzed via X-ray diffraction without requiring crystallization of the molecule itself.
This advancement is expected to accelerate pharmaceutical research by enabling structure determination of compounds that are difficult to crystallize or available only in small amounts.
New Quantum State Physicists from Rice University and Vienna University of Technology discovered a topological semimetal phase in CeRu4Sn6 at near absolute zero temperature. The state emerged through quantum criticality and was identified via an unusual Hall effect without an external magnetic field.
The finding challenges previous assumptions: strong electron interactions can create, not destroy, topological states . This insight could inform advances in quantum computing, electronic efficiencies, and sensing technologies by revealing new mechanisms for engineering topological quantum materials.
Material Key Property Significance High-entropy borides High magnetic anisotropy Rare-earth-free magnets APF-80 MOF Robust structure Drug discovery tool CeRu4Sn6 Topological semimetal phase Quantum applications AI Tools Accelerate Discovery Faster Molecular Design Researchers from NYU and the University of Florida developed PropMolFlow , an AI model that designs molecules with specified properties 10 times faster than previous methods. The system reduces computational steps from 1,000 to 100 while maintaining 90% accuracy for generating chemically valid structures.
The method works backward from desired properties to molecular structures, validated using physics-based density functional theory. This “inverse design” approach accelerates discovery for pharmaceuticals and materials by directly targeting specific characteristics rather than screening large libraries. The work was published in Nature Computational Science in January 2026.
Human-AI Collaboration Argonne National Laboratory and the University of Chicago developed an AI advisor model for autonomous labs that enables collaborative decision-making between humans and AI. Applied to the Polybot self-driving lab, the system created a mixed ion-electron conducting polymer with a 150% performance improvement over previous methods.
The approach combines human expertise with AI’s data-processing capabilities, allowing researchers to guide autonomous experiments while leveraging machine learning for optimization. The team published their findings in Nature Chemical Engineering in December 2025.
Quantum Machine Learning Researchers from the University of Maryland and IonQ demonstrated that quantum kernel machine learning outperforms classical methods in navigating materials phase space using less experimental data. The study, conducted on IonQ’s Aria trapped-ion quantum computer, used X-ray diffraction patterns from an Fe-Ga-Pd alloy library.
The work provides experimental evidence for quantum advantage in materials discovery, particularly when working with complex diffraction data and limited experimental samples . The findings suggest quantum computing could accelerate autonomous experimentation in materials science.
Method Key Metric Application Autonomous AI Network 3 systems collaborated Materials optimization PropMolFlow 10x faster, 100 steps Molecular design AI Advisor 150% performance gain Autonomous labs Quantum Kernel ML Less data needed Phase space navigation Data Infrastructure NIMS developed Research Data Express (RDE) , a flexible data management system designed to standardize and automate materials science data processing. Since its 2023 launch, the platform has seen significant adoption: 5,000 users , 1,900 Dataset Templates implemented, 16,000 datasets created, and 3 million accumulated data files .
RDE uses customizable Dataset Templates to interpret data from various experiments, reducing researchers’ data processing burden and promoting FAIR data principles. The system serves as key infrastructure for Japan’s national materials science initiatives, addressing the critical bottleneck of inconsistent and siloed data that hampers collaborative research and AI-driven discovery.
Funding and Industry Moves TU/e secured $1.5 million euros as part of the $6 million euro Horizon Europe project SimuLingua, which aims to develop a next-generation AI platform for materials discovery. The project will create a multimodal scientific foundation model enabling researchers to explore materials via natural language and AI-accelerated simulations.
Novyte Materials raised pre-seed funding led by Theia Ventures to support its AI-driven materials discovery platform. The company aims to cut R&D time by up to 10x and reduce testing costs by 90%.
South Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT announced a $275.4 billion won investment in the 2026 Nano and Materials R&D Project, focusing on securing core materials technologies and integrating AI to accelerate research.
Energy Fuels is acquiring Australian Strategic Materials for approximately $447 million AUD, highlighting strategic moves to secure critical minerals supply chains and reduce dependence on China for rare earth processing.
Also This Week Pablo Jarillo-Herrero (MIT) and Allan MacDonald (University of Texas) won the BBVA Foundation Frontiers of Knowledge Award for their discovery of the “magic angle” in graphene layers. Their work on twistronics—rotating graphene at 1.1 degrees to control electronic properties—has applications in quantum computing and energy-efficient AI.
The Materials Project has been cited 32,000 times and serves 650,000 users, accelerating research in batteries and quantum computing. The platform provides high-throughput computational modeling and AI-ready datasets, with 99.98% uptime on its cloud infrastructure.

content:
D-Wave completed its acquisition of Quantum Circuits Inc. for $550 million, becoming the first company to offer both annealing and gate-based quantum systems. Meanwhile, IBM researchers demonstrated that today’s noisy quantum computers can reliably study complex physics using a 91-qubit processor with advanced error mitigation.
D-Wave Creates First Dual-Platform Quantum Company D-Wave finalized its $550 million acquisition of Quantum Circuits Inc., positioning itself as the only company offering both annealing and gate-model quantum computing systems. The deal, structured as $300 million in stock and $250 million in cash , brings together two distinct approaches to quantum computing: annealing systems excel at optimization problems, while gate-model systems are general-purpose quantum computers suitable for a wider range of algorithms.
The acquisition gives D-Wave access to Quantum Circuits’ dual-rail qubit technology , which reduces the physical qubit overhead for fault-tolerant systems by up to 200 times. This error-detecting architecture uses two physical modes to represent quantum information, offering built-in error detection that could significantly accelerate the path to practical quantum computing.
D-Wave plans to release a 49-qubit gate-model system in 2026 , complementing its existing Advantage annealing platform. The company will establish a new R&D center in New Haven, Connecticut, and Dr. Rob Schoelkopf , Quantum Circuits’ co-founder and Yale professor, joins as Chief Scientist.
Technical Breakthroughs IBM Demonstrates Reliable Quantum Simulations IBM researchers used a 91-qubit superconducting processor to accurately reproduce signatures of quantum chaos, demonstrating that current noisy quantum computers can provide reliable scientific insights before fault-tolerant machines arrive. The study, published in Nature, executed 4,000 two-qubit gates using dual-unitary circuits designed to benchmark complex many-body physics.
The key to achieving reliable results was tensor-network error mitigation (TEM) , an advanced technique that reduces the impact of noise on quantum computations without requiring full error correction. The researchers tested system sizes ranging from 51 to 91 qubits and completed the entire workflow in 3 hours , demonstrating practical near-term quantum utility.
The work shows that error-mitigated quantum simulation can adjudicate between conflicting classical methods for complex physics problems, providing a credible path for scientific value from pre-fault-tolerant quantum computers.
Alice & Bob’s Error Correction Advance Alice & Bob unveiled “Elevator Codes,” a novel error correction method for its cat qubit quantum computers that promises a 10,000x lower logical error rate while requiring only about 3x more qubits compared to its current error correction approach.
The technique uses code concatenation to make a logical ancilla qubit operate like an elevator within repetition codes, enabling detection of bit-flips at the logical level. Cat qubits already suppress phase-flip errors through their biased noise characteristics, and Elevator Codes address the remaining bit-flip errors with remarkable efficiency. This advancement could dramatically reduce the overhead of error correction, making large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computations more attainable.
Open-Source Quantum Computing Initiative The University of Waterloo launched Open Quantum Design (OQD) , a non-profit organization hosting the world’s first open-source, full-stack quantum computer using trapped-ion technology. The initiative has attracted 30 software contributors and aims to accelerate progress by providing open access to hardware and software for algorithm testing and workforce training.
OQD represents a collaborative third path distinct from traditional academic labs and commercial startups, with partners including Haiqu and Xanadu. The project builds on eight years of computing hardware development at the Institute for Quantum Computing.
Security Vulnerabilities Identified Penn State researchers warned about security flaws in quantum computers themselves, highlighting vulnerabilities in both software and hardware. The study identified issues including crosstalk and lack of program integrity verification that could make quantum systems targets for cyberattacks. The researchers urge developers to safeguard quantum systems from the ground up as the technology moves toward wider use.
Quantum Threats to Cryptocurrency The cryptocurrency industry is grappling with quantum computing’s potential threat to cryptographic security. Jefferies, a global investment banking firm, removed its 10% Bitcoin allocation from its model portfolio, with strategist Christopher Wood citing quantum computing as a potential threat to Bitcoin’s cryptographic foundations. The allocation was shifted to physical gold and gold mining stocks.
Coinbase responded by forming an Independent Advisory Board on Quantum Computing and Blockchain , bringing together experts including quantum computing pioneer Scott Aaronson, Stanford cryptography expert Dan Boneh, and Ethereum researcher Justin Drake. The board will assess risks, publish position papers, and recommend best practices, with its first paper expected in early 2027.
Meanwhile, quantum-software firm BlueQubit launched a public challenge offering 0.25 BTC ($22,500) to anyone who can solve a cryptographic problem. The company claims its quantum computer can find the hidden private key in under two hours, while classical supercomputers would take years.
Market Activity Rigetti Computing secured an $8.4 million order from India’s Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC) for a 108-qubit quantum computer . The system will be installed on-premises in Bengaluru with deployment scheduled for H2 2026 , building on an existing partnership and highlighting growing demand for on-premises quantum computers.
Montana State University’s QCORE received a $31.5 million contract from the Air Force Research Laboratory to advance quantum infrastructure. The funding will expand quantum networking test beds, integrate advanced sensors and computing architectures, and accelerate commercialization of quantum technologies. This builds on a prior $26.7 million grant awarded in 2023.
Chinese quantum computing company SpinQ Technology closed a Series C funding round , raising hundreds of millions of RMB (roughly $14-40 million USD) led by Longli Technology and Jadex Capital. The funds will advance the company’s full-stack quantum systems and expand its global footprint.
Irish startup Equal1 raised $60 million to scale its silicon-based quantum computing systems. The funding will accelerate rollout of its Bell-1 quantum server and scale manufacturing using existing semiconductor foundries, focusing on standard CMOS fabrication to lower cost and deployment barriers.
Microsoft released an updated open-source Quantum Development Kit that streamlines fault-tolerant quantum application development. The kit includes specialized tools for chemistry modeling and error correction, with AI-assisted coding and support for multiple quantum frameworks including Q#, OpenQASM, Qiskit, and Cirq.
Policy and Infrastructure Rep. Chuck Fleischmann of Tennessee advocated for increased federal investment in quantum computing, AI, and supercomputing, arguing they are critical for U.S. national security and global leadership. The congressman warned that adversaries like China are heavily investing in these technologies and positioned Tennessee to play a leading role through involvement with the Department of Energy and all 17 national lab directors.
Ohio State Representative Heidi Workman introduced House Bill 650 to establish the Frontier Technologies and Quantum Computing Commission. The bipartisan commission will study emerging technologies like AI, quantum computing, and biotechnology to inform policy and position Ohio as an innovation leader while addressing economic, ethical, and security implications.
Europe launched the $50 million Photonics for Quantum (P4Q) pilot line to industrialize quantum photonic chips. The project, coordinated by the University of Twente with 29 partners across 12 countries, aims to develop standardized production techniques for photonic chips used in quantum computing, sensing, and secure communication.
What to Watch This week’s developments reflect steady progress across multiple fronts. D-Wave’s dual-platform strategy signals industry maturation, with companies recognizing that different quantum computing approaches serve different applications. The acquisition brings together optimization-focused annealing systems with general-purpose gate-model computing, creating a more comprehensive offering for customers.
Error correction and mitigation techniques continue advancing, with IBM demonstrating practical near-term utility through tensor-network error mitigation and Alice & Bob achieving dramatic efficiency gains with Elevator Codes. These advances show progress toward practical systems without requiring full fault-tolerant quantum computers.
The cryptocurrency debate highlights real-world security concerns as quantum computing capabilities grow. While the timeline for quantum threats to current cryptography remains uncertain, the industry response—from Jefferies’ portfolio adjustment to Coinbase’s advisory board—demonstrates increasing awareness and preparation.
Geographic spread of activity is notable, with significant developments in India (Rigetti’s $8.4M order), China (SpinQ’s Series C), Europe (€50M photonics pilot line), and the United States (Montana State’s $31.5M contract). This international competition is driving both investment and policy attention.
Key milestones ahead include D-Wave’s 49-qubit gate-model system in 2026, Rigetti’s India deployment in H2 2026, and Microsoft’s full error correction suite expected in late 2026. These concrete deliverables will test whether the industry can transition from research demonstrations to commercial deployment.

content:
The 2022 ChatGPT Moment When ChatGPT was announced at the end of 2022, I spent hours talking to it, genuinely amazed at how it was a step up compared to the previous GPT-3 models (davinci, curie, if those ring a bell). Around that time, I had been on-and-off playing with LangChain to build tool-using agents. While the agents felt unreliable, they made for great demo-ware. The pace of innovation was staggering. The LangChain team shipped new features in a matter of hours, a sign that the AI space was heating up fast.
For the next few weeks, I was playing with ChatGPT almost non-stop, with mixed feelings. Hallucination was real, and it was really hard to get the 3.5-turbo models to follow instructions reliably. It constantly made up wrong citations and could not do simple math. Even GPT-4 could not count the number of letters in a word.
Building Copilot for Chemistry At the time, I was working on Azure Quantum Elements, which aimed to bring together HPC, AI, and quantum computing for scientific discovery. We had data and models for molecules and materials, so it was natural to try LangChain’s ReAct agent for coordinating the execution of those tools. The agent worked well when the problem space and user’s questions matched the narrow fields it was designed for.
Based on the demo’s promise, we realized this seemed to be the future. We rallied a team to intensely work on developing Copilot in Azure Quantum for chemistry and materials. Around the same time, the ChemCrow (Bran et al., 2023) paper came out, and the results gave us a lot of confidence.
We announced Azure Quantum Elements and the Copilot in June 2023 (Zander, 2023). It was a really fun time when a small group of us worked day and night, including weekends for months to make that happen, navigating the responsible AI process along the way. Nobody was asked to work overtime, but everyone was always online to deploy, test, and fix things fast.
Looking back, we had a few good ideas that were probably ahead of their time. We had a rendering window for molecules and calculation results. Later people invented a new term for this UX, namely “Generative UI.” In the scientific field, we deal with big data objects in addition to text responses. Passing large calculation data was nontrivial, and we invented a new way to do that given the limited context of language models.
Workflow vs Agent In an ideal world, I envisioned that the service would evolve into what we now call an “AI Scientist.” The reality is like many early AI services: the churn rate was high. It was reasonably popular for some time, then user engagement dropped and it no longer made sense to maintain. To this date, the only thing I could quickly find was in this blog post (Chen & Almulla, 2023). AI (even with GPT-4, the best model at the time) was still not great at understanding human instructions, and the system was not very reliable, as people reported edge cases all the time. We tried to automate the tests, but the APIs were slow and those are more like regression tests, instead of trying to predict what new queries users may come up with. Again, if we were to build it today, the development of LLM evaluation field and automated red teaming would help us solve some of those.
This made us wonder if a workflow-based system would make more sense. The LangChain blog had a nice analysis on this topic (Chase, 2025).
Obviously, people in the AI space realized this earlier than we did, and LangGraph was developed to address these reliability concerns using more deterministic execution graphs (perhaps also fixing the confusing interface from LangChain). The concept of agentic workflows was later integrated into Microsoft’s Agentic Framework, after a few branding iterations and mergers with other tools like Semantic Kernel, AutoGen, etc. (Microsoft, 2025).
The Reasoning Revolution Beyond the reliability issues, we also realized something deeper was missing. A scientific process (or arguably any complex task) requires more than a chatbot. They require more of “System 2” thinking (slow/deliberate/reflective processes) than “System 1” thinking (fast/automatic/intuitive processes) (Kahneman, 2011).
The famous Chain-of-Thought paper (Wei et al., 2022) was groundbreaking, albeit simple. By eliciting reasoning steps, language models like ChatGPT were able to achieve better results, mimicking how humans work. Then there were several very interesting prompting techniques. Something I recall trying with a colleague was adding “take a deep breath” from DeepMind (Yang et al., 2023). It’s funny, but in some cases it worked.
The o-series reasoning models from OpenAI made a splash. They pioneered test-time compute and extended the chain-of-thought idea by spending more tokens to achieve much better results. This unlocked so many doors and was perhaps a key moment for AI in scientific discovery.
I was switching between ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude around that time. Then Deep Research from both Gemini and ChatGPT really won me over as a user, and Claude was just in its own league for software engineering tasks. I ended up paying for all of them to this day. It seemed inches away to connect deep research with automated software engineering for autonomous research engineering work.
The Rise of AI Scientists and the Return of Agents While many teams were looking into deterministic workflows due to reliability concerns, the rapid improvements in reasoning capabilities quietly made fully autonomous agents viable again. While Microsoft was pitching the concept of “Copilot”, a related concept of “AI (co-)Scientist” took off. It started with Gomes’ team publishing their results on Coscientist in (Boiko et al., 2023). Later, Google shared their AI co-Scientist (Gottweis et al., 2025), and fast forward to recent news where FutureHouse released Kosmos after a few product iterations (Mitchener et al., 2025).
The fundamental idea is surprisingly simple. In some way, it is running reasoning and tool calling in a loop. Lilian Weng’s blog (Weng, 2023) is a great resource on the high-level concepts. But of course, building a reliable one is extremely hard, something we faced every day during the Copilot development.
With frontier AI labs pushing intelligence forward, the distinction between workflows and AI agents becomes blurrier. I personally found, particularly in the last few months, that agentic systems can achieve fairly reliable execution while being more flexible across many tasks. I started to truly feel that we are entering the agentic era from the chatbot generative AI era. Jensen Huang was definitely right on this.
The Copilot for Chemistry initiative was not completely lost. Earlier this year, Microsoft Discovery (Microsoft, 2025) was announced, pushing to build an agentic platform for science. My previous work on AI-accelerated battery electrolyte discovery (Chen et al., 2024) was used as an example of how AI can help accelerate scientific discovery. AI brings unique value to science.
What’s Next? One big trend in 2025 was seeing startups in AI for materials science or physical AI companies with a heavy component in materials raising big funding rounds, again reiterating Jensen’s vision about the future of physical AI. The Genesis Mission executive order (The White House, 2025) pushes the heat to another level. It all makes a lot of sense, as materials and engineering serve as the building blocks for our society. From my past work in this space, it was very clear to me that AI is going to help discover a lot of materials, and it is only a matter of execution, validation, and scale. Perhaps this by itself will be another blog post at a later stage.
The data question is becoming central: the whole internet’s data is somewhat exhausted, so you would need to generate synthetic data or experimental data. Lots of experiments in science, if you capture all the data, can be extremely valuable if one knows how to merge that data with existing data and figure out a path towards scientific superintelligence.
This is likely where quantum computing enters the picture. As I work in the quantum computing industry, I see a natural connection: materials and molecules fundamentally operate on quantum mechanics principles, which classical computers struggle to simulate accurately. Quantum computers could generate training data that captures physics classical systems cannot, potentially unlocking new frontiers for AI in science. 2026 is going to be another exciting year for AI for Science.
What I Learned If I had to summarize what the past few years taught me:
We kept hitting reliability problems, not capability problems. The demos were always impressive, but getting things to work in production was a different story. Users found edge cases we never thought of, and maintenance became a full-time job that few want to take.
The reasoning models (o1, o3) were the unlock. Before that, we were patching unreliable systems with workflows. After that, agents actually started working.
We went from agents to workflows and back to agents. It felt like going in circles, but the second time around, the agents were better. Sometimes you have to retreat before you can advance.
And now everyone is talking about data. The internet is tapped out. Science has data that nobody else has, and that might be the edge. The nice part about science is that you can validate in real world.
Final Words I have long hoped to build an agent that can automate myself. Deep Research was probably the first tool that I felt was powerful enough to replace part of myself for literature review and information gathering. The barrier to entering a new field has never been lower. During the break, I decided to build an agent for writing research review articles for me. The following is a 148-page zero-shot generation (plus answering the clarification questions) of my “literature-reviewer” agent using the prompt “Impacts and potentials of quantum computing for artificial intelligence”.
If you’re curious about how quantum computing can help build better AI, take a look:
Impacts and Potentials of Quantum Computing for Artificial Intelligence: A Comprehensive Review
It is not perfect, but it is a fitting way to close 2025. A year where the tools we dreamed of building finally started building themselves.

The 2022 ChatGPT Moment

When ChatGPT was announced at the end of 2022, I spent hours talking to it, genuinely amazed at how it was a step up compared to the previous GPT-3 models (davinci, curie, if those ring a bell). Around that time, I had been on-and-off playing with LangChain to build tool-using agents. While the agents felt unreliable, they made for great demo-ware. The pace of innovation was staggering. The LangChain team shipped new features in a matter of hours, a sign that the AI space was heating up fast.
